title: Contentment, not complacency
hook: santokh is peace with what is, while still acting

segments.voice: Yesterday, humility in practice: on Guru Nanak's scale, the side that bows is the heavier one. Your line was strength that doesn't show. Did you let one small win go, and keep quiet about it? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-six.

Morning on the bank of the Ravi, and a man walks out with the farmers to work the soil. Tradition says this is Guru Nanak in his later years, at Kartarpur, the town where he settled after his long journeys. The teacher of the Japji, out plowing. He could have sat and received offerings. Instead, the story goes, he worked the land, and the community ate together from what it grew. That picture holds today's word in both hands: a deep peace with what is, and a plow still moving. Contentment.

First, the word. Santokh: contentment, enough, the end of the restless more. A few days ago, Asa di Var put it in a chariot: in Satjug, the hymn says, contentment was the chariot. Second, why it matters so much. In the Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase: without contentment, no one is satisfied; like dreams, every wish and every effort comes to nothing. Notice the target. Not wanting things. Being satisfied. A person can get everything on the list and still feel hungry, because the list was never the hunger. Santokh cuts the hunger itself. Third, the trap on the other side. Contentment could slide into complacency: I'm fine, the world's fine, why bother. The Gurus close that door. In a salok, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: the one who eats what they earn by their own effort, and gives some of it from their own hand, Nanak, that one recognizes the way. Earn. Give. Both are verbs. Contentment, in the Sikh picture, is not a couch. It's the peace of someone who works hard, takes what comes, shares it, and isn't eaten up by wanting more. Fourth, the field again. Guru Nanak at Kartarpur, as tradition tells it, is the picture: content enough to need no throne, active enough to plow. So santokh doesn't ask a student to stop studying, or a worker to stop asking for a fair wage, or anyone to stop fighting injustice. It asks them to do all that without the gnawing. Peace with what is, while still acting. That's the difference between contentment and complacency: complacency stops the hands. Contentment only quiets the hunger.
screen: `SANTOKH: THE END OF THE RESTLESS MORE.` · `WITHOUT CONTENTMENT, NO ONE IS FULL.` · `EARN BY EFFORT, GIVE FROM YOUR HAND.` · `QUIET THE HUNGER, NOT THE HANDS.` · then, large: `CONTENT AND WORKING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be content and still work. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you're working toward. A goal, a project, a raise, a skill. On the in-breath, say inside: this is enough, right now. On the out-breath: and I'll keep working. Notice if one half fights the other, or comes more easily. Just let both sit side by side, like the farmer's peace and the farmer's plow. The bell holds the time.
Contentment. Santokh: peace with what is, the end of the gnawing for more, held together with honest work and sharing. Today's word.
Your line: content and working. Today, do one task fully, as well as you can, and when it's done, stop and call it enough before reaching for the next. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs count santokh, contentment, among the core virtues and pair it with kirat karni, honest work, and vand chhakna, sharing what is earned.
